questions.stem: Which article do German nouns ending in „-chen“ take, like Mädchen (girl), Brötchen (bread roll), Kaninchen (rabbit)?
questions.explanation: Every noun ending in „-chen“ takes „das“ — Mädchen (girl), Brötchen (bread roll), Kaninchen (rabbit) — and it makes the word a smaller version of something. Roughly a third of German nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do German nouns ending in „-ung“ take, like Zeitung (newspaper), Wohnung (flat), Übung (exercise)?
questions.explanation: Every noun ending in „-ung“ takes „die“ — Zeitung (newspaper), Wohnung (flat), Übung (exercise) — and there are no exceptions. Roughly a third of German nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do German nouns ending in „-heit“ take, like Freiheit (freedom), Krankheit (illness), Schönheit (beauty)?
questions.explanation: Every noun ending in „-heit“ takes „die“ — Freiheit (freedom), Krankheit (illness), Schönheit (beauty) — and it usually turns an adjective into a noun. Roughly a third of German nouns announce their gender in the ending, which is the closest thing to a shortcut the language offers.

questions.stem: Which article do German nouns ending in „-keit“ take, like Möglichkeit (possibility), Schwierigkeit (difficulty)?

questions.stem: Which article do the days of the week take?
questions.explanation: Days, months and seasons are all masculine: der Montag, der Januar, der Sommer. It is one of the few gender rules with no exceptions to learn.

questions.stem: „Das Mädchen“ means 'the girl'. Why is it neuter?
options: It is an exception with no reason
Because it is a plural form
Nouns ending in -chen are always neuter
All nouns for children are neuter
questions.explanation: The -chen ending makes a diminutive and forces the word neuter, whatever it means. Grammatical gender and real-world gender are different things, and this is the clearest proof of it.

questions.stem: What happens to a German verb used as a noun, like „das Essen“?
options: It becomes neuter and takes a capital letter
questions.explanation: Any infinitive can be turned into a noun — „essen“ (to eat) becomes „das Essen“ (food, or the meal). It is always neuter and always capitalised, which makes it a reliable way to build vocabulary you already half know.

questions.stem: Which of these nouns is feminine?
questions.explanation: „Wohnung“ ends in -ung, so it is feminine regardless of what the rest of the word looks like. The others take their gender from their final element: der Ort, das Zimmer, der Wagen.

questions.stem: In a compound noun like „das Fußballspiel“, which part decides the gender?
questions.explanation: The final element decides: „das Spiel“ is neuter, so „das Fußballspiel“ is too, even though „der Fußball“ is masculine. That one rule makes German's long compounds far less frightening than they look.
